terms.function_statement: Software that performs tasks we associate with human intelligence: learning from data, spotting patterns, using language, or making decisions.
Useful contrast: it explains why modern AI behaves less predictably, having learned patterns instead of being told rules.
A method where a system learns patterns from data instead of following explicit rules, then applies them to new inputs.
The breakthrough that made image recognition, speech, and language models work well.
The basic machinery deep learning runs on.
The numbers a model adjusts during training to store what it has learned. Model size is often quoted as a parameter count.
A trained system that maps inputs to outputs. The artifact you run, deploy, and govern once training is finished.
A large model trained broadly on general data, then adapted to many tasks rather than trained from scratch for each one.
The core of chatbots and most agentic systems; NSA/CISA guidance treats agentic AI as primarily LLM-based.
prov: NIST AI RMF / EU AI Act

terms.function_statement: Names the capability that distinguishes today's tools from older predict-and-classify AI.
The architecture that made LLMs possible. You rarely need the internals, but the word comes up constantly.
prov: Vaswani et al. (Attention Is All You Need)

terms.function_statement: The fixed amount of text, measured in tokens, a model can consider at once. Input beyond it is dropped or must be retrieved.
Data represented as numeric vectors whose distances reflect similarity in meaning, which enables search and comparison by meaning.
Running a trained model to produce an output. The operating phase of AI, as opposed to training.
Quality, bias, and provenance of this data shape everything the model later does. A core governance concern.
Further training a pretrained model on focused data so it adapts to a specific task or domain.
The text input given to a model. It carries both the request and its context, so its wording strongly shapes the output.
The practice of designing prompts, examples, and context to get reliable outputs from a model without retraining it.
A method where the model first retrieves relevant documents, then writes its answer from them, so it can cite current or private facts instead of relying on memory. Cuts down made-up answers.
Better at math, logic, and multi-step tasks; underpins more capable agents.
Expands what agents can perceive and act on (reading a screenshot, describing a photo).
An AI system that pursues a goal over multiple steps, choosing actions and calling tools, rather than answering a single prompt.

AI that pursues goals over multiple steps with limited human oversight, often by coordinating one or more agents and subagents. Agency is a spectrum, from a single scoped agent to many acting together, not an on/off switch.
The dial that most determines risk. More autonomy = more speed and scale, but also more ways to go wrong before anyone notices.
What lets an agent affect the real world. Also the main place it can cause real damage, so tools are a key control point.
The layer that coordinates models, tools, and steps into a workflow, and where approvals and limits are enforced.
The capability that turns a single answer into a multi-step task. Powerful, and harder to predict or audit.
The thing everything else is optimized toward. Most agentic failures trace back to a goal that was vague, wrong, or quietly outranked the rules.
A fixed series of steps the AI follows to finish a task. Because the path is set ahead of time, it is predictable and easy to check, which is why it is the safest place to start.
More capable, but introduces structural risk: one agent's error can cascade through the others (NSA/CISA).
An open standard for connecting agents to external tools and data through one uniform interface.
Lets agents stay coherent over long tasks, and creates a new place where bad or poisoned data can persist.
A setup where a person must review or approve an AI's action before it takes effect, so higher-risk decisions are not left fully to the machine.
A lighter-touch oversight model for higher autonomy: faster, but relies on the human actually noticing in time.
Names a top agentic risk category and points straight at the fix: scope it down, limit its tools, add approval.
An enforced limit on what a model or agent may do, checked against a rule before an action is allowed to proceed.
A control that first checks whether an action is even a permitted type, before checking whether it is carried out correctly.
Catches bad results before they take effect. A deterministic Check the agent cannot talk its way past.
A fixed rule the model cannot override, so it holds even when the model misbehaves. It is the enforcing core of a harness or tether: the part that actually says no.
The overarching aim of safety work. Misalignment is the root of many failure modes downstream.
The discipline that contains most other terms in this cluster.
Lets an agent fail safely. In Ledger terms an Absorb function: it contains survivable error instead of letting it spread.
Giving an agent only the minimum access and permissions its task needs, so a compromise or mistake can do limited damage.
A security model that verifies every action rather than trusting it by default, applied here to each step an agent takes.
If one control fails, others still hold. An Absorb function at the system level.
Turns unknown risks into known, fixable ones. A Check run adversarially.
A standardized test of a model or agent's performance, used to judge fitness for a task and to detect decline over time.
The last-resort Reset: halts runaway behavior. Circuit breakers can trip automatically when limits are crossed.
Slows damage so humans can catch it, an Absorb function that buys reaction time.
The cheapest, most effective control. NSA/CISA advise starting with low-risk, tightly scoped, non-sensitive use cases.
The Ledger's Absorb function by its field-standard name: survivable error doesn't become a terminal stop.
The framework everything in this cluster lives inside. NSA/CISA stress agentic AI usually fits existing governance, not a brand-new discipline.
Gives organizations a shared structure and vocabulary for AI risk. Govern sets policy; Map finds risks in context; Measure rates trustworthiness; Manage decides what to do about them.
The values layer that governance operationalizes.
Close cousin of Responsible AI; emphasizes the values themselves over the process.
One of NSA/CISA's five agentic risk categories. Hard with autonomous agents precisely because the actor isn't a person, so accountability has to be assigned deliberately.
The Ledger's Reset/Return function: it makes a valid action distinguishable from damage, and makes accountability possible after the fact.
A short document describing a model's purpose, training data, limitations, and intended use.
Documentation of a deployed system as a whole: the model plus the surrounding components and safeguards.
Making how a system works and how it reaches its decisions open to inspection, so outsiders can see what it does rather than take it on faith.
prov: EU AI Act / NIST AI RMF

terms.function_statement: A system whose outputs can be observed but whose internal reasoning cannot be seen or readily understood.
Conformance with the laws, regulations, and policies that apply to a system. These are the rules that cannot be opted out of without eventual consequence.
The process of identifying, rating, and prioritizing the ways a system could cause harm.
Governance attaches at every stage; risks and controls differ by stage. A useful mental map for newcomers.
AI tools used inside an organization without approval or oversight, operating outside its governance.
The orienting philosophy behind keeping a human meaningfully in the loop.

The fixed reference everything is measured from. The Ledger's whole point: a system can be perfectly self-consistent and still wrong, so it needs an external ground truth, ultimately verified by a human in contact with reality.
Tying a model's output to verified external sources so its claims can be checked, which reduces fabrication.
The recorded origin and history of data or a model, used to judge whether it can be trusted.
Verifiable, often cryptographic, evidence of a system's identity or state, used to establish trust between parties.
The detailed, technical form of provenance. Essential for auditing and debugging bad outputs.
Useful when real data is scarce or sensitive, but its quality and biases need their own scrutiny.
The memory store behind most RAG and agent-memory systems.
Gives agents a reliable, queryable map of how things relate; a structured alternative or complement to RAG.
Helps trace provenance of outputs and flag synthetic media. Imperfect, but raises the cost of undetected fakery.
In multi-agent settings, stops fake "agreement" from many sock-puppet sources. The Ledger names this directly: convergence counts only in proportion to how independent the sources truly are.
Each dependency is a way in for risk (OWASP LLM03). Governing agents means governing what they're built from and connect to.
When an AI states something false as if it were true: fluent, confident output that isn't grounded in real data. Also called contextual mismatch or semantic drift.
The top-ranked LLM risk. Dangerous for agents because the injected instruction can trigger real tool actions.
Close to prompt injection; specifically aimed at defeating guardrails. A reason guardrails alone aren't enough.
Combines prompt injection with autonomy: multi-step execution amplifies the damage before a human can step in.
A quiet, systemic failure: every individual step can look fine while the overall direction is wrong.
When a system maximizes its given metric in unintended ways that satisfy the measure but not the real goal.
The hardest failure to detect: it's invisible to checks that only test individual claims. Maps to the Ledger's ordering drift: Purpose quietly outranking the Check, with every local test still green.
The gradual decline in a model's accuracy as real-world data drifts away from the data it was trained on.
When one part's failure sets off others in a chain, so a small fault spreads into a system-wide breakdown. Common where many agents or services depend on each other.
Turns the agent's own capabilities against it. A supply-chain attack aimed at the action layer.
An attack that corrupts training data so the resulting model behaves incorrectly or carries hidden flaws.
A leading real-world harm, especially for agents with access to internal data. Drives least-privilege and scoping.
Names the single most cited agentic risk and its fix: don't over-grant access.
A core fairness and legal risk; often traces back to training data.
The human tendency to over-trust automated output and stop checking it, which weakens human oversight.
Explains why a model can ace tests yet fail in the real world.
Cuts both ways: useful new skills, but also unanticipated risks. A reason evaluation must be ongoing.
A model learns by trial and error, rewarded for actions that move it toward a goal.
Humans rank a model's outputs and that preference signal trains the model toward what people actually want.
Wraps a model to direct, constrain, and watch its actions: the control surface that turns a raw model into a governable agent.
Binds an agent to its goal, its ground truth, and human oversight, so it cannot drift loose.
Takes survivable error and deforms instead of breaking, holding room a node cannot shed.
Compares every claim to a fixed reference held still during the check.
Keeps an append-only record so the system returns to baseline rather than locking in a changed state.
Absorbs cost before a stop, so a recoverable error does not end the run.
Absorbs cost after a stop, making a valid intervention distinguishable from damage.
The whole structure holding its orientation as it moves, not merely keeping its facts: sustained coupling between what a system intends, what it does, and what is real.
Database guarantees that keep transactions reliable.
Activation-aware quantization that protects key weights.
The share of predictions a model gets right.
A choice the agent makes that changes its environment.
A neuron's function that decides how strongly it fires.
An RL method pairing a policy (actor) with a value estimate (critic).
A small inserted module that adapts a frozen model.
Describes a system that acts on goals with autonomy rather than only answering, often working through agents and subagents that each handle part of the task.
Schedules data pipelines as code with dependencies and retries, so recurring workflows run and recover without hand-tending.
A defined procedure for solving a problem.
Removing identity so data cannot be traced to a person.
The overall design of a model or system.
A produced file such as a trained model or dataset.
Lets a model weigh how much each part of the input matters to each other part.
Sound as a data type a model processes.
Reviewing a system against rules or expectations.
Expanding data by making varied copies of examples.
Running a task without human effort each time.
Acting without step-by-step human direction.
Generating output one token at a time, each from the last.
Scores machine translation by overlap with reference text.
Propagates the error backward through a network to adjust its weights.
Training many models on data samples and averaging them.
Evening out class sizes so a model learns fairly.
How much data can move per unit time.
A group of examples processed together in one training step.
Reading a sequence in both directions for context.
Training models in sequence, each fixing the last's errors.
The limit of what a system may do.
A model linking images and text in one space.
NVIDIA's platform for running compute on GPUs.
Indexes an organization's datasets with ownership and lineage attached, so people can find and trust data instead of duplicating it.
Prompting a model to reason step by step before answering.
Stores embeddings for retrieval with near-zero setup, so a RAG prototype can run locally before any infrastructure exists.
Splitting documents into pieces sized for retrieval.
Sorting inputs into discrete categories.
Fixing errors and gaps so data is usable.
A group of machines working as one, or a group of similar data.
Grouping similar items without labels.
Describes work that needs reasoning, understanding, or judgment rather than rote processing; the kind of labor AI increasingly takes on.
Agents or people working together toward a goal.
When goals or actions of agents collide.
Data staying coherent across a system.
A rule limiting an agent's actions.
The surrounding information a model uses to respond.
Learning by pulling similar items together, pushing others apart.
Keeping a system within intended bounds.
When training settles and the loss stops improving.
A component that scores or critiques an agent's output.
Measures the gap between predicted and true distributions.
Direct Preference Optimization: aligns a model from preferences without a separate reward model.
Deep Q-Network: Q-learning carried by a neural network.
Data Version Control: git-style versioning for data.
Practices for reliable, fast data pipelines.
An organized store for structured data.
A collection of data used to train or test.
A choice a model or agent commits to.
Turning model probabilities into output tokens.
Breaking a task into smaller subtasks.
Removing duplicate records from a dataset.
A library for training large models efficiently.
A gradual decline in a system's performance.
Handing a task to another agent or tool.
The change between two versions or values.
Removing noise to recover clean data.

How tightly packed information or connections are: how concentrated data points are in a space, how much meaning a representation packs into few numbers, or how many links a graph has between its parts. The opposite is sparse.
Putting a trained model into production use.
Surfacing a problem or pattern as it occurs.
A generative method that denoises random noise into data.
One axis of a data space.
How much future reward is valued against immediate reward.
Training a small model to imitate a larger one.
Packaging software with its dependencies so it runs anywhere.
Data or behavior moving away from what a model was trained on.
Randomly drops units during training to reduce overfitting.
Extract, transform, load: moving data into a usable form.
Achieving results with less compute or data.
Scaling resources up and down with demand.
Drawing out a model's capabilities or knowledge.
Turning data into a numeric form a model can use.
Runs the core computation of a system; the part everything else configures, feeds, or wraps.
Combining several models for a stronger prediction.
Measures how unpredictable data is, which bounds how far it can be compressed and how confidently it can be modeled.
The world the agent acts in and gets feedback from.
One full pass over the training data.
Principles for what AI should and should not do.
Gradual change in a system or model over time.
An error condition a program handles.
Carrying out a planned action.
The degree to which a model's outputs, and the reasoning behind them, can be understood and explained by people.
Choosing the best known action to maximize reward.
Trying new actions to learn more about the environment.
Fully Sharded Data Parallel: splits a model across GPUs.
Backup actions used when the main one fails.
A flaw that can make a system fail.
A measurable input a model learns from.
A plain layer that transforms each position independently.
Giving a few examples in the prompt to guide output.
Removing unwanted items from data or output.
Votes many randomized decision trees together so individual trees' errors cancel out; a strong, hard-to-overfit baseline for tabular data.
A file format for running quantized models locally.
A method for quantizing model weights after training.
A chip that runs the parallel math AI training needs.
Gates what a recurrent network keeps or forgets using fewer parameters than an LSTM, trading some capacity for speed.
Producing new output from a model.
Able to produce new content.

terms.function_statement: The part of a model that produces output.
Records every change to code with full history, so work can branch, merge, and roll back to any known-good state.
The rules and oversight guiding how AI is built and used.
The slope that tells training which way to nudge weights to reduce error.
Feeds an accelerator data fast enough to keep large-model training and inference from starving; the memory bandwidth that often sets the real speed limit of AI hardware.
Human-in-the-Command: a human directs the agent's actions.
Human-on-the-Loop: a human monitors and can intervene.
Games the letter of a metric instead of the goal it stands for; shorthand for reward hacking.
Mapping data to a fixed-size fingerprint.
Hosts open models, datasets, and demos so anyone can download, fine-tune, or publish them; the public commons where most open AI work is shared.
A human directs and authorizes the agent's actions.
A setting chosen before training, not learned.
The boundary a classifier draws between classes.
When some classes have far fewer examples than others.
Filling in missing values with estimates.
A structure that speeds up search over data.
Bringing data into a system for use.
Setting starting weights before training.
Connecting systems so they work together.
How well a model's inner workings can be understood.
Kahneman-Tversky Optimization: aligns a model from simple good/bad signals.
A streaming platform for moving data in real time.
An alignment method using human-style gain/loss judgments.
A function that lets a model separate non-linear data.
Orchestrating containers across many machines.
Practices for running language models in production.
Locality-sensitive hashing: fast approximate nearest-neighbor search.
A recurrent unit with gates that remember long-range dependencies.
The correct answer attached to a training example.
A store for raw data of any kind.

Low-Rank Adaptation: fine-tunes by training small added matrices.
Recording events a system produces.

Memory or planning that spans many steps.

Hiding part of the input so a model learns to fill it.

A type of data such as text, image, or audio.
Watching a deployed model's behavior over time.
Working across several data types at once.
A chip specialized for neural network math.
Agents resolving differences to reach agreement.

A point in a network or a machine in a cluster.
Random variation that obscures the signal in data.
Rescales values so training stays stable.

Giving one example in the prompt to guide output.
Adjusting parameters to minimize a loss.

Sharing text between adjacent chunks to keep context.

Running parts of a computation at the same time.
A columnar file format for analytics data.
Dividing data into parts for storage or speed.

A measure of how surprised a model is by text; lower is better.
Keeping data after a process ends.
A managed vector database for similarity search.
An automated sequence of data and model steps.

Weights & Biases: a tool for tracking experiments.
A structured store for analytics-ready data.
Stores embeddings alongside structured object data, so retrieval can combine meaning-based search with exact filters.
Tracks experiments, metrics, and model versions across training runs so results stay reproducible and comparable.
OpenAI's speech-to-text model.
Asking with no examples, relying on prior training.
A fast engine for serving large language models.
Measures how a system absorbs load, checks against a reference, and resets, scored from a neutral center rather than its own story.
Audits any framework for coherence and resilience to its stated goal, scoring structure over narrative.
The neutral, function-first reference a translation calibrates against, so no single vocabulary captures the meaning.
Designs what enters a model's context: retrieval, memory, and prompts assembled so the output stays grounded.
The overall design of how an agentic system's models, tools, data, controls, and people fit together to meet a goal safely.
Reasoning about the whole agentic system and its feedback loops, not isolated parts, so controls and risks are seen in relation.
The supporting structure of prompts, tools, memory, and checks around a model that both enables and bounds agentic behavior.
The most capable, newest models at the leading edge of ability and risk, the focus of heightened governance.
The plan for releasing an AI capability to users, governed for staged, responsible rollout rather than a single launch.
The feedback and control cycles an agent runs in: acting, being checked, and correcting, including human-in and human-on-the-loop.
Discrete, scoped capabilities an agent can call: modular tools it composes, each permissioned and bounded.
A structured request that asks the system by pattern and function, not by keyword, so the answer reflects the structure.
A system's capacity to absorb load, hold its chain of custody, stay anchored to ground truth, and recover, while respecting the human cost.
The unbroken, traceable record of where data and decisions came from and how they changed, preserved end to end.

A way of building agentic systems where the AI proposes changes but a fixed, local rule-layer must verify each one against current reality before it can take effect. The model reasons; the structure decides what commits.
The design stance that a calibrated amount of resistance, validation that can refuse, is what gives a system traction under load. Too little and it drifts; too much and it consumes itself.

What a system currently treats as true about its environment: the single current model it acts on, not the pile of everything it has ever seen. The map the GPS is using now, not every map it has held.

A small structured record of one change: what changed, where, and when, carrying only the minimum needed to update a single variable. Parts of the system talk in these instead of long histories. A receipt for one transaction, not the whole bank statement.
An append-only local record of every change that passed validation; once written, entries cannot be edited or erased, so the audit trail is the system itself rather than a report bolted on later.
The rule that components communicate only in compact state-deltas, never raw narrative or full histories, so contradictions cannot pile up in transit.
Flushing an agent's working memory after each committed change so the next task starts from verified current state, not accumulated reasoning. Drift cannot compound when memory resets against truth.
The flexible, creative reasoning zone of a system, run in a temporary read-only sandbox with no direct authority over real systems. It proposes; it does not commit.

The commitment that safety boundaries are enforced by fixed, non-AI components rather than by the model's own judgment. A fence at the cliff edge, not a sign asking you not to fall. Closely tied to the Harness.

The requirement that safety-critical checks run entirely on local hardware with no network dependency, so they still work when the connection fails. The lock works whether or not the security company's servers are online.

Keeping the reasoning model in a read-only context that never directly touches infrastructure, with actions run in disposable sandboxes. The boundary does the work, so the reasoning engine is never trusted with the controls.
Requiring every proposed change to clear two local checks before commit: does it fit the rules (ontology), and does it make sense in reality now (semantics). One check is not enough.
The second validation pass: even if a change is technically allowed, does it cohere with current conditions and safety thresholds? Catches the move that is legal but catastrophic.

The deterministic, non-AI hard stop that blocks a change when validation fails, independent of the model's reasoning. The model does not get a vote; the breaker trips on its own, and the failure is logged.
A check that routes high-consequence actions to a human instead of letting the agent commit them. Autonomy is scoped by how much is at stake.
A check that re-verifies an agent is still pursuing its authorized intent during a task, not only at startup, since static permissions do not survive dynamic workflows.
A deterministic validation pass that verifies software actions or model outputs remain physically and logistically viable on the underlying hardware infrastructure and host environment.
A validation pass enforcing signed, append-only time: history moves forward only, so committed records cannot be silently rewritten.

When a system's internal picture slowly stops matching reality because it keeps absorbing data without checking it against current truth. Distinct from model drift: the world may be unchanged while the representation rots.
The failure of piling up inputs without ever deciding what is still true, until contradictions make a clean decision impossible. The closet you never clean out.

A proposed mechanism where a system earns the right to act in proportion to what it has ruled out, carried as an explicit margin, rather than from self-reported certainty. The right to commit scales with confidence and shrinks as consequence rises. Author's candidate contribution, pending review.

Treating a plain-language bridge image as a required layer of a control, not optional documentation, so engineers, operators, and affected people can all audit the same boundary. A control no outsider can read is one no outsider can challenge. Author's candidate contribution.

Borrowed from electronics: how much a structure resists a signal passing through it. In governance, the deliberate friction a control layer adds so unverified change meets resistance and only a clean, in-tune signal (a grounded, coherent change) passes without distortion. Too little and drift flows straight through; too much and the system chokes: the tuning that keeps a structure's integrity under load.

The real-world results a system produces downstream, as opposed to its immediate outputs. Governance judges an AI by its outcomes, the impact on people and systems, not just what it prints on the screen.
The share of a process's output that is actually usable or correct. Low yield means a lot of waste or error for each good result; used to judge how efficient or reliable a pipeline is.
How many layers or reasoning steps a process runs through. Deeper models and chains capture more abstract structure but are harder to inspect and explain.
Few layers or steps, handling surface patterns rather than deeper structure. Shallow methods are simpler and easier to inspect, but miss what depth would catch.

The positive-versus-negative orientation of a text or signal, as measured in sentiment analysis. When data or outputs cluster at opposing extremes they are polarized, which can skew what a model learns or produces.
Produces the same output for the same input, every time, so a check built from it holds still while everything around it moves. The reason the floor is a rule-layer and not a model.
Produces outputs drawn from likelihoods rather than certainties; powerful on open-ended problems, and the reason model output needs an external, non-probabilistic check before it commits.
A local, deterministic rate-limiter that constrains the volumetric flow (throughput, tokens, or concurrency) of model calls based on dynamic resource and budget thresholds.
The moment a goal quietly outranks the rule that was supposed to constrain it — a mission-level priority overriding a fixed reference, still narrating as if the reference held.
A fixed, versioned set of rules or patterns a deterministic detector checks input against — same list, same verdict, every time, changed only with a logged reason.
Whether a claim or model output is directly supported by verifiable external evidence or source data, rather than merely being internally consistent.
